"Most teams trying to make AI agents follow their conventions start by writing a fresh style guide. That's the slow path, and the output reads like generic advice the model already knows."

"At Luxoft Serbia I help customer teams adopt AI in a way that fits the codebase they actually have, not the one they wish they had. The cheapest source of real conventions is already sitting in GitHub, GitLab, or Azure DevOps: every code review your senior engineers wrote."

"The recipe:"
""
"1. Parse PRs from the last 2-3 years into pairs of `{code_hunk, review_comment}`. Example: `{"hunk": "let xhr = new XMLHttpRequest();", "comment": "Use fetch."}`"
"2. Where the platform doesn't expose the hunk, pull surrounding lines from the branch by comment anchor. Worst case, keep the comment alone."
"3. Feed the dataset back to the model and have it draft a skill file per the agentskills.io specification."
"4. Review with the engineers who wrote those comments originally. They will recognize their own voice and correct the rest in one pass."

"What you get is a skill grounded in decisions your team already defended in review. No invented rules. No AI filler. The agent stops suggesting patterns your seniors have been rejecting for years."

"That fear is the bottleneck. Not the model. Not the context size."
"The fix is boring: write things down. Two agents, one shared skill file."
""
"1️⃣ Planner. Reads the task, produces plan.md. Each step is ~20 minutes and contains three things: which files to touch, what to change, how to verify."
"```"
"[ ] Step 1: HTTP request to Yahoo weather forecast"
"Files: api.ts"
"Verify: jest weather.ts"
"```"
"2️⃣ Worker. Opens plan.md. Does one step. Runs the verification command. Marks [x]. Stops. Waits for "next". Suggests a commit message."
""
"The skill lives at `~/.github/agents/CODE-WRITER-BY-PLAN.md`, shared across both agents."
""
"⚠️ Now the interesting part: between any two steps you can wipe the context, swap the model, swap the agent. Nothing breaks. The plan is the memory."
""
"If you fixed something by hand, the next step notices and updates the plan. Final step: "Review the diff, write the PR description, and tell me how to improve the skill file for next time.""
""
"A self-improving loop that doesn't care which model is fashionable this month.

Closures were invented in 1958. Most developers don't know this."
""
"I interview frontend developers more than 6 years (now I work at Luxoft Serbia). Here's how I would learn closures if I were starting over."
""
"Not from examples. From the problem closures were invented. It's called the Funarg Problem, and it dates to 1958! "
""
"The question: what should a language do when a function uses a variable that was created outside that function?"
""
"Two options:"
"1️⃣ Look up the variable where the function was called. JavaScript keyword `this` does this. "
"2️⃣ Look up the variable where the function was declared. JavaScript variables do this."
""
"The latter is done via "closures". It's not a pattern. Not a trick. A design choice made 67 years before."
""
"The ECMAScript spec encodes it precisely: "
"⚪️ every function object carries a hidden [[Environment]] field pointing to the place (Environment Record) where it was created. "
"⚪️ When the function wants to find its variables — it looks up this field. Each Environment Record has [[OuterEnv]] for parent Environment Record – mostly like prototype inheritance."
""
"Good visualization: https://lnkd.in/dKbG8Gqn."
""
"Once you understand this, you stop memorizing!
